result.markdown:
# Principal Components

[Slides for this lecture](40-principal-components_slides.html)



::: {.callout-tip}
### Learning objectives
After this lecture you should be able to

- **define** the loading vector $\phi_1$ and the scores $z_{i1}$ of the first
principal component, and **derive** $\phi_1$ as the eigenvector of the sample
correlation matrix with the largest eigenvalue, by maximizing the sample
variance of the scores subject to $\left\|\phi_1\right\| = 1$,
- **explain** why the first principal component is also the line closest to
the standardized data, in average squared distance,
- **describe** the later components as orthogonal directions of decreasing
variance, **compute** the proportion of variance explained by each component
and cumulatively, and **choose** a number of components $M$ from a scree plot
or a cumulative rule, stating why the choice is a judgment,
- **explain** why the features are standardized before principal component
analysis, and **predict** which explanatory variable dominates the first
component when they are not,
- **interpret** the loadings and scores of a component, including why the sign
of a loading vector is arbitrary, and
- **explain** why principal component analysis is unsupervised, why it is not
variable selection, and why the component with the most variance need not be
the best predictor of a response.
:::

Subset selection, ridge regression, and the lasso fit a model to all $p$
features and control its flexibility by keeping some of the
features or by shrinking the coefficient estimates. Dimension reduction instead
replaces the $p$ features by $M < p$ linear combinations of them and fits a
model to those. Here $M$ is the number of components kept; in the ridge and
lasso lectures it was the number of repeated training samples. This lecture
constructs the linear combinations, the principal components; the next one
regresses on them. Principal component analysis is the subject of ISLR2
Chapter 12, which the course reaches after Exam 2.

## Diamond measurements

### Data

**Question.** Diamonds are described by six numbers: weight, two proportions,
and three physical dimensions. Can fewer than six directions capture most of
the variation in these numbers?

**Data.** `ggplot2::diamonds` records 53,940 diamonds. The
response variable is the price, `price`, in US dollars, which this lecture
does not use. The numeric explanatory variables are

- `carat`, the weight (one carat is 200 mg),
- `depth`, the total depth percentage, the height of the diamond as a
percentage of its average width, $100z/\left[(x + y)/2\right]$, computed from
the three dimensions below,
- `table`, the width of the flat top facet as a percentage of the widest
point, and
- `x`, `y`, and `z`, the length, width, and depth in mm.

`cut`, `color`, and `clarity` are ordered categories with no numeric scale, so
they have no variance or correlation in the sense used below and are left out.

### Recording errors

The figure plots the width `y` and the depth `z` against the length `x` for
all 53,940 diamonds.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The numeric explanatory variables, and the largest plausible dimension.
features <- c("carat", "depth", "table", "x", "y", "z")
max_mm <- 20

# Flag diamonds with a zero dimension or a dimension above max_mm.
status_levels <- c("Kept", "Removed")
diamonds_flagged <- diamonds |>
  mutate(zero = x == 0 | y == 0 | z == 0,
         extreme = !zero & (x > max_mm | y > max_mm | z > max_mm),
         status = if_else(zero | extreme, "Removed", "Kept"),
         status = factor(status, levels = status_levels))

# Zero dimensions, and diamonds removed for each reason.
n_zero <- c(x = sum(diamonds$x == 0),
            y = sum(diamonds$y == 0),
            z = sum(diamonds$z == 0))
n_zero_rows <- sum(diamonds_flagged$zero)
n_extreme <- sum(diamonds_flagged$extreme)

# The retained diamonds, their number n, and the number of features p.
kept <- diamonds_flagged |>
  filter(status == "Kept") |>
  select(-zero, -extreme, -status)
n <- nrow(kept)
p <- length(features)
largest_kept <- max(kept[c("x", "y", "z")])

# Dimensions above max_mm, and the other dimensions of those diamonds.
dims <- as.matrix(diamonds[c("x", "y", "z")])
n_big_values <- sum(dims > max_mm)
big_rows <- dims[diamonds_flagged$extreme, , drop = FALSE]
big_others <- big_rows[big_rows <= max_mm]
big_widths <- sort(diamonds$y[diamonds$y > max_mm], decreasing = TRUE)

# Width and depth against length, one panel each, removed diamonds on top.
dimension_labels <- c("Width y (mm)", "Depth z (mm)")
n_diamonds <- nrow(diamonds)
cleaning_title <- paste(big(n_diamonds), "diamonds")
cleaning_plot <- diamonds_flagged |>
  pivot_longer(c(y, z), names_to = "dimension", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(dimension = if_else(dimension == "y",
                             "Width y (mm)",
                             "Depth z (mm)"),
         dimension = factor(dimension, levels = dimension_labels)) |>
  arrange(status) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value, color = status, shape = status)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ dimension) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("grey40", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17)) +
  labs(x = "Length x (mm)",
       y = NULL,
       color = NULL,
       shape = NULL,
       title = cleaning_title) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Most diamonds lie close to the line width = length, and depth rises with
length. 8 diamonds have length 0, 7 width 0,
and 20 depth 0, 20 diamonds in all; a physical
dimension of 0 mm is impossible. There are 3 values above
20 mm: widths of
58.9 and 31.8 mm
and a depth of 31.8 mm, on diamonds whose other
dimensions are 5.12 to 8.09 mm. A
handful of other diamonds sit away from the cloud, below it in the depth
panel, but their values are possible.

The rule used here removes every diamond with a dimension of 0 or larger than
20 mm: 23 diamonds
(20 with a zero, 3 with an extreme value), leaving
$n = 53{,}917$. The largest remaining dimension is
10.74 mm. Every computation below uses all $n$ retained
diamonds; the scatterplots show a random subsample of them.

### Correlated measurements


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Retained diamonds drawn at random for the scatterplots.
n_sub <- 1000
sub_id <- sample(n, n_sub)

# The number of them shown in the two-feature figures.
n_shown <- 250
```
:::


The lower panels of the scatterplot matrix plot each pair of explanatory
variables for 1,000 diamonds drawn at random from the retained ones,
the first random draw after `set.seed(20261021)`. The upper panels give the
correlations over all $n$ retained diamonds.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Explanatory variables as a matrix, their correlations, and the subsample.
X <- as.matrix(kept[features])
cor_X <- cor(X)
X_sub <- X[sub_id, ]

# Plot titles for all retained diamonds and for the subsample.
title_all <- paste(big(n), "retained diamonds")
title_sub <- paste(big(n_sub), "retained diamonds")

# Midpoint of each variable's range in the subsample, where text is placed.
sub_min <- apply(X_sub, 2, min)
sub_max <- apply(X_sub, 2, max)
mid <- (sub_min + sub_max) / 2

# Panel column and row variables as factors, in the order of features.
as_grid <- function(d) {
  mutate(d,
         xvar = factor(xvar, levels = features),
         yvar = factor(yvar, levels = features))
}

# Lower panels: the subsampled points of each pair of variables.
pair_index <- combn(p, 2)
pair_points <- function(k) {
  first <- pair_index[1, k]
  second <- pair_index[2, k]
  tibble(xvar = features[first],
         yvar = features[second],
         xval = X_sub[, first],
         yval = X_sub[, second])
}
n_pairs <- ncol(pair_index)
lower <- map(seq_len(n_pairs), pair_points) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  as_grid()

# Upper panels: the correlation over all n retained diamonds.
upper_x <- features[pair_index[2, ]]
upper_y <- features[pair_index[1, ]]
upper_r <- cor_X[cbind(upper_x, upper_y)]
upper <- tibble(xvar = upper_x,
                yvar = upper_y,
                xval = mid[upper_x],
                yval = mid[upper_y],
                label = fmt_math(upper_r)) |>
  as_grid()

# Diagonal panels: each carries its variable's range, so every row and
# column has a scale, and its name and unit.
diagonal_points <- function(f) {
  tibble(xvar = f, yvar = f, xval = X_sub[, f], yval = X_sub[, f])
}
diagonal <- map(features, diagonal_points) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  as_grid()
units <- c(carat = "carats",
           depth = "%",
           table = "%",
           x = "mm",
           y = "mm",
           z = "mm")
diagonal_text <- tibble(xvar = features,
                        yvar = features,
                        xval = mid,
                        yval = mid,
                        label = paste0(features, "\n(", units, ")")) |>
  as_grid()

# Scatterplot matrix: points below the diagonal, correlations above it.
pairs_caption <- paste("Upper panels: correlations over all",
                       big(n),
                       "retained diamonds.")
pairs_plot <- ggplot(lower, aes(x = xval, y = yval)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.5) +
  geom_blank(data = diagonal) +
  geom_text(data = upper, aes(label = label), size = 5) +
  geom_text(data = diagonal_text,
            aes(label = label),
            size = 4,
            fontface = "bold") +
  facet_grid(yvar ~ xvar, scales = "free", switch = "both") +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = NULL,
       title = title_sub,
       caption = pairs_caption) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside",
        axis.text = element_text(size = 7))

# Correlations among the four size variables, and of depth and table with
# them.
size_vars <- c("carat", "x", "y", "z")
size_cors <- cor_X[size_vars, size_vars][upper.tri(diag(4))]
other_cors <- cor_X[c("depth", "table"), size_vars]
```
:::

![](40-principal-components_files/figure-html/pairs-figure-1.png){width=816}

:::


Carat, length, width, and depth in mm rise together: their correlations are
0.98 to 1.00. Length, width, and depth
are close to linear in one another, and carat curves upward against each of
them, since weight grows with volume. Depth percentage and table are nearly
unrelated to these four (correlations −0.03 to
0.20) and weakly to each other
(−0.30). Four of the six explanatory variables are
close to one measurement, the size of the diamond.

Depth percentage is not a separate measurement.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Recorded depth percentage against the one computed from the dimensions.
average_width <- (kept$x + kept$y) / 2
depth_computed <- 100 * kept$z / average_width
depth_gap <- abs(kept$depth - depth_computed)
```
:::


Over the $n$ retained diamonds, recorded `depth` differs from
$100z/\left[(x + y)/2\right]$ by a median of 0.03
percentage points, the size of the rounding in the recorded values; only
77 diamonds differ by more than 1 point, the largest by
44.5 points. The six explanatory variables therefore carry five
measurements: weight, table, and the three dimensions. Depth percentage is
nearly uncorrelated with size because it records the depth `z` relative to
`x` and `y`, a shape, not a size.

### Features

The features are the standardized explanatory variables,

$$\tilde x_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \bar x_j}{s_j}, \qquad s_j = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(x_{ij} - \bar x_j\right)^2},$$

where

- $x_{ij}$ is explanatory variable $j = 1, \ldots, p$ of diamond
$i = 1, \ldots, n$, in the order `carat`, `depth`, `table`, `x`, `y`, and `z`, so $p = 6$,
- $\bar x_j$ and $s_j$ are the mean and the standard deviation (divisor $n$)
of explanatory variable $j$, as in the [Ridge
Regression](20-ridge-regression.qmd) lecture, and
- $\tilde x_{ij}$ is feature $j$ of diamond $i$; $\tilde{\mathbf{X}}$ is the
$n \times p$ matrix of features and $\tilde x_i$ its row $i$.

Each feature has mean 0 and $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\tilde x_{ij}^2 = 1$, and

$$\mathbf{R} = \frac{1}{n}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}}$$

is the $p \times p$ sample correlation matrix, whose entries are the upper
panels of the scatterplot matrix. The bold $\mathbf{R}$ is a matrix and is
unrelated to the coefficient of determination $R^2$, which appears once, in
the section on price. The section on scaling shows what happens without
standardization.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Standard deviation with divisor n.
sd_n <- function(v) {
  deviations <- v - mean(v)
  sqrt(mean(deviations^2))
}

# Standardized features and their correlation matrix R.
X_std <- scale(X, center = TRUE, scale = apply(X, 2, sd_n))
R <- crossprod(X_std) / n
```
:::


## First principal component

### Two features

The first figure plots standardized table against standardized depth for
the first 250 diamonds of the subsample. The other tabs add a direction
through the origin and each diamond's perpendicular projection onto it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Standardized depth and table, and their correlation.
X_dt <- X_std[, c("depth", "table")]
r_dt <- cor_X["depth", "table"]

# Unit direction at angle theta, in degrees from the depth axis.
direction <- function(theta) {
  radians <- theta * pi / 180
  c(cos(radians), sin(radians))
}

# Variance, over all n diamonds, of the scores along direction theta.
score_variance <- function(theta) {
  mean((X_dt %*% direction(theta))^2)
}

# For each angle: the variance of the scores and the mean squared distance
# to the line.
theta_grid <- 0:180
mean_sq_length <- mean(rowSums(X_dt^2))
theta_curves <- tibble(theta = theta_grid,
                       variance = map_dbl(theta_grid, score_variance),
                       distance = mean_sq_length - variance)
theta_best <- theta_curves$theta[which.max(theta_curves$variance)]

# Value of one column of theta_curves at one angle.
at_theta <- function(theta, col) {
  theta_curves[[col]][theta_curves$theta == theta]
}

# Base plot: the first n_shown diamonds of the subsample.
shown <- as_tibble(X_dt[sub_id[seq_len(n_shown)], ])
dt_caption <- paste("Variance and mean squared distance over all",
                    big(n),
                    "retained diamonds.")
dt_base <- ggplot(shown, aes(x = depth, y = table)) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-4, 4), ylim = c(-4, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Standardized depth",
       y = "Standardized table",
       title = paste(n_shown, "retained diamonds"),
       caption = dt_caption)

# The line at angle theta and each diamond's projection onto it.
dt_projection <- function(theta) {
  a <- direction(theta)
  proj <- mutate(shown,
                 score = depth * a[1] + table * a[2],
                 depth_p = score * a[1],
                 table_p = score * a[2])
  variance <- fmt(at_theta(theta, "variance"))
  distance <- fmt(at_theta(theta, "distance"))
  subtitle <- paste0("Angle ",
                     theta,
                     " degrees: score variance ",
                     variance,
                     ", mean squared distance ",
                     distance)
  dt_base +
    geom_abline(slope = a[2] / a[1],
                intercept = 0,
                color = "#D55E00",
                linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_segment(data = proj,
                 aes(xend = depth_p, yend = table_p),
                 color = "#0072B2",
                 alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
    labs(subtitle = subtitle)
}

# Tabs: the data, the depth axis, and the first principal component.
dt_data <- dt_base +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  labs(caption = NULL)
dt_plots <- list(dt_data,
                 dt_projection(0),
                 dt_projection(theta_best))

# Both quantities against the angle, the two angles above dotted.
theta_title <- paste(big(n), "retained diamonds, standardized depth and table")
theta_plot <- theta_curves |>
  pivot_longer(-theta, names_to = "quantity") |>
  mutate(quantity = if_else(quantity == "variance",
                            "Variance of the scores",
                            "Mean squared distance to the line")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = theta, y = value, color = quantity, linetype = quantity)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, theta_best),
             color = "grey60",
             linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(4, 5)]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 180, by = 45)) +
  labs(x = "Angle of the direction (degrees from the depth axis)",
       y = NULL,
       color = NULL,
       linetype = NULL,
       title = theta_title) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The cloud is tilted down to the right, the negative correlation
$r = -0.30$ between depth and table. Projected onto the depth
axis, the diamonds' positions along the line have variance
1.00, the variance of standardized depth. Along
the line at 135 degrees, which runs with the tilt, they spread
more, variance 1.30, and the projection
segments are shorter. The last tab sweeps the direction through every angle:
the variance of the positions along the line is largest at the same angle at
which the mean squared distance to the line is smallest.

### Loadings and scores

The **first principal component** of the features is the linear combination

$$Z_1 = \phi_{11}\tilde X_1 + \phi_{21}\tilde X_2 + \cdots + \phi_{p1}\tilde X_p, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^p\phi_{j1}^2 = 1,$$

with the largest sample variance, where

- $\tilde X_j$ is feature $j$, the standardized explanatory variable,
- $\phi_{j1}$ is the **loading** of feature $j$ on the first component, and
$\phi_1 = \left(\phi_{11}, \ldots, \phi_{p1}\right)^\top$ is the **loading
vector**, a unit-length direction in the $p$-dimensional feature space (not
the dispersion parameter $\phi$ of the [Generalized Linear
Models](../04-classification/70-generalized-linear-models.qmd) lecture), and
- the value of $Z_1$ for diamond $i$,

$$z_{i1} = \sum_{j=1}^p\phi_{j1}\tilde x_{ij} = \tilde x_i\phi_1,$$

is its **score** on the first component, its signed position along the
direction $\phi_1$. The $n$-vector of scores is $z_1 = \tilde{\mathbf{X}}\phi_1$.

Without the constraint $\left\|\phi_1\right\| = 1$ the variance could be made
as large as desired by multiplying the loadings by a constant. In the
two-feature figure, the line at angle $\theta$ has unit direction
$a = \left(\cos\theta, \sin\theta\right)^\top$, each blue segment ends at
the projection $\left(\tilde x_ia\right)a^\top$ of a diamond onto it, and the
first component is the line with the largest variance of $\tilde x_ia$.

### Maximum variance

The features have mean 0, so the scores of any unit vector $a$ have mean 0
and sample variance

$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\tilde x_i a\right)^2 = \frac{1}{n}a^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}}a = a^\top\mathbf{R}a.$$

To maximize $a^\top\mathbf{R}a$ subject to $a^\top a = 1$, introduce a
Lagrange multiplier $v$ and set the gradient of
$a^\top\mathbf{R}a - v\left(a^\top a - 1\right)$ to zero:

$$2\mathbf{R}a - 2va = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathbf{R}a = va.$$

So a maximizing direction is an eigenvector of $\mathbf{R}$ with eigenvalue
$v$, and multiplying $\mathbf{R}a = va$ on the left by $a^\top$ shows that the
variance of its scores is $a^\top\mathbf{R}a = va^\top a = v$. Of all the
unit eigenvectors, the one with the largest eigenvalue gives the largest
variance: **$\phi_1$ is the eigenvector of the sample correlation matrix with
the largest eigenvalue $v_1$, and $v_1$ is the variance of the first
component's scores.** Both are estimates, computed from the $n$ diamonds, of
the leading eigenvector and eigenvalue of the population correlation matrix of
the explanatory variables.

For two features,
$\mathbf{R} = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}1 & r\\ r & 1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$
and

$$a^\top\mathbf{R}a = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta + 2r\cos\theta\sin\theta = 1 + r\sin 2\theta.$$

With $r < 0$ it is largest at $\theta = 135$ degrees, where it equals
$1 + |r| = 1.30$: the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{R}$ are
$1 \pm r$, with eigenvectors $\left(1, 1\right)^\top/\sqrt 2$ and
$\left(1, -1\right)^\top/\sqrt 2$. For two standardized features with
$r \ne 0$, the first principal component is always one of the two 45-degree
lines; the correlation decides which one and how much variance it carries.
With $r = 0$ the eigenvalues tie and every direction is a first component.

### Closest line

Because $\phi_1$ has unit length, Pythagoras splits each diamond's squared
distance from the origin into its squared score and its squared distance from
the line:

$$\left\|\tilde x_i\right\|^2 = z_{i1}^2 + \left\|\tilde x_i - z_{i1}\phi_1^\top\right\|^2.$$

Averaging over the diamonds, and using $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i\tilde x_{ij}^2 = 1$
for each of the $p$ features,

$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left\|\tilde x_i - z_{i1}\phi_1^\top\right\|^2 = p - \phi_1^\top\mathbf{R}\phi_1.$$

The left side is the mean squared distance from the diamonds to the line
through the origin in direction $\phi_1$, and it is $p$ minus the variance of
the scores. The direction that maximizes the variance therefore minimizes the
mean squared distance: the first principal component is also the line closest
to the data. In the last tab the two curves sum to $p = 2$ at every angle.

### Six features


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Eigendecomposition of the correlation matrix.
eig <- eigen(R, symmetric = TRUE)

# Sign of the largest entry of phi in absolute value.
largest_sign <- function(phi) {
  largest <- which.max(abs(phi))
  sign(phi[largest])
}

# Loading vectors, each signed so its largest loading in absolute value is
# positive.
flip <- apply(eig$vectors, 2, largest_sign)
Phi <- sweep(eig$vectors, 2, flip, "*")
dimnames(Phi) <- list(features, paste0("PC", 1:p))

# Component variances and the n x p matrix of scores.
v <- eig$values
Z <- X_std %*% Phi

# Largest correlation between two columns of scores, in absolute value.
score_cors <- cor(Z)[upper.tri(diag(p))]
max_score_cor <- max(abs(score_cors))
```
:::


For all six features, the eigenvector of $\mathbf{R}$ with the largest
eigenvalue is the estimated loading vector

$$\phi_1 = \left(0.49, 0.00, 0.12, 0.50, 0.50, 0.50\right)^\top,$$

in the order `carat`, `depth`, `table`, `x`, `y`, and `z`, with $v_1 = 4.00$.
The scores $z_{i1}$ have variance 4.00, against 1 for any single
feature.

## Later components

### Remaining variation

The figure shows, for each feature, the distribution of
$\tilde x_{ij} - z_{i1}\phi_{j1}$ over the $n$ diamonds: what is left of the
feature after its part along the first component is removed.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# What is left of each feature after its first-component part is removed.
residual_1 <- X_std - Z[, 1] %o% Phi[, 1]
remaining_var <- colMeans(residual_1^2)

# Violins of the remainders, cut at 5 in absolute value.
n_cut_remaining <- sum(abs(residual_1) > 5)
remaining_caption <- paste("Lines = quartiles and median;",
                           n_cut_remaining,
                           "values above 5 in absolute value are not shown.")
remaining_plot <- as_tibble(residual_1) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature") |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = features)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = feature, y = value)) +
  violin +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-5, 5)) +
  labs(x = "Feature",
       y = "Standardized value minus its first-component part",
       title = title_all,
       caption = remaining_caption)
```
:::

The four size features have almost nothing left: their remaining variances

theirs, 1.000 and 0.943. The next
direction should be found mostly in depth and table.

### Orthogonal directions

The **$m$th principal component** $Z_m$, with loading vector $\phi_m$ and
scores $z_{im} = \tilde x_i\phi_m$, maximizes the sample variance of the
scores among unit vectors orthogonal to $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_{m-1}$, for
$m = 2, \ldots, p$.

The eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix $\mathbf{R}$ can be chosen
orthonormal. Order them by their eigenvalues
$v_1 \ge v_2 \ge \cdots \ge v_p \ge 0$, and assume no ties. Any unit vector is
$a = \sum_{m=1}^p c_m\phi_m$ with $\sum_m c_m^2 = 1$, and since
$\mathbf{R}\phi_m = v_m\phi_m$,

$$a^\top\mathbf{R}a = \sum_{m=1}^p c_m^2v_m,$$

a weighted average of the eigenvalues. Orthogonality to
$\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_{m-1}$ forces $c_1 = \cdots = c_{m-1} = 0$, and the
largest weighted average of $v_m, \ldots, v_p$ puts all the weight on $v_m$.
So $\phi_m$ is the eigenvector with the $m$th largest eigenvalue, and the
scores of the $m$th component have variance $v_m$. All $p$ components come
from one eigendecomposition.

Two properties follow.

- **The scores are uncorrelated.** For $m \ne l$, the sample covariance of
$z_m$ and $z_l$ is
$\frac{1}{n}\phi_m^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\phi_l = \phi_m^\top\mathbf{R}\phi_l = v_l\phi_m^\top\phi_l = 0$.
- **The variances add up to $p$.** With $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ the $p \times p$
matrix whose columns are $\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_p$, which is orthogonal,
$\sum_m v_m = \operatorname{tr}\left(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(\mathbf{R}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^\top\right) = \operatorname{tr}\left(\mathbf{R}\right) = p$,
the total variance of the standardized features.

For the diamonds the sum of the six eigenvalues is 6.00, and the
largest correlation between two columns of scores is
$2.9 \times 10^{-11}$ in absolute value.

### prcomp

`prcomp()` with `scale. = TRUE` computes the same components.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Principal components from prcomp().
pca <- prcomp(X, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

# Largest differences from the eigendecomposition, up to sign.
loading_gap <- abs(pca$rotation) - abs(Phi)
loading_diff <- max(abs(loading_gap))
variance_diff <- max(abs(pca$sdev^2 - v))
score_gap <- abs(pca$x) - sqrt((n - 1) / n) * abs(Z)
score_diff <- max(abs(score_gap))
```
:::


Up to sign, its loadings `pca$rotation` agree with the eigenvectors of
$\mathbf{R}$ to within $1.4 \times 10^{-10}$. `prcomp()` standardizes with
divisor $n - 1$, so its scores `pca$x` are $\sqrt{(n - 1)/n}$ times the scores
here (to within $6.3 \times 10^{-10}$). Its variances `pca$sdev^2`, computed
with divisor $n - 1$ as well, equal the eigenvalues $v_m$ (to within
$6.3 \times 10^{-13}$), because the two factors cancel. Its signs are
whatever its algorithm returns.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Beyond this course
- **Singular value decomposition.** `prcomp()` does not form $\mathbf{R}$. It
computes the singular value decomposition
$\tilde{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{V}^\top$, whose right
singular vectors (the columns of $\mathbf{V}$) are the loading vectors and
whose squared singular values divided by $n$ are the variances $v_m$; this is
more accurate numerically than an eigendecomposition of $\mathbf{R}$.
- **Best low-dimensional approximation.** The closest-line property extends:
the first $M$ components span the $M$-dimensional subspace closest to the
data in mean squared distance, and $\sum_{m=1}^M z_{im}\phi_m^\top$ is the
best rank-$M$ approximation of $\tilde{\mathbf{X}}$.
- **Variants.** Sparse principal components force some loadings to zero, much
as the lasso does for coefficient estimates; kernel principal components find
nonlinear directions; robust principal components limit the influence of
outlying observations.
:::

### Variance explained

The **proportion of variance explained** by component $m$ is

$$\text{PVE}_m = \frac{v_m}{\sum_{l=1}^p v_l} = \frac{v_m}{p},$$

where $v_m$ is the variance of the $m$th component's scores and the
denominator is the total variance of the standardized features. The
cumulative PVE of the first $M$ components is
$\sum_{m=1}^M\text{PVE}_m$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Proportion of variance explained by each component, and cumulatively.
pve <- v / sum(v)
cum_pve <- cumsum(pve)

# Table of the variances and proportions.
pve_tibble <- tibble(Component = paste0("PC", 1:p),
                     `Variance $v_m$` = fmt(v, 3),
                     `PVE` = pct(pve, 2),
                     `Cumulative PVE` = pct(cum_pve, 2))
pve_table <- knitr::kable(pve_tibble, align = "lrrr")

# Scree plot and cumulative PVE, with the 90% level dotted.
scree_types <- c("Component m (scree plot)",
                 "First m components (cumulative)")
type_rep <- rep(scree_types, each = p)
scree_data <- tibble(m = rep(1:p, 2),
                     value = c(pve, cum_pve),
                     type = factor(type_rep, levels = scree_types))
scree_plot <- ggplot(scree_data,
                     aes(x = m,
                         y = value,
                         color = type,
                         shape = type,
                         linetype = type)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.9, color = "grey50", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(4, 5)]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:p) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Component m",
       y = "Proportion of variance explained",
       color = NULL,
       shape = NULL,
       linetype = NULL,
       title = title_all) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# The component after which the PVE drops by the largest factor.
M_elbow <- which.max(pve[-p] / pve[-1])

# The fewest components whose cumulative PVE reaches 90%.
M_90 <- which(cum_pve >= 0.9)[1]
```

### Components kept

Keeping the first $M$ components replaces the $p$ features by $M$ new
variables, the columns of scores $z_1, \ldots, z_M$; $M$ is the dimension of
the reduced feature set. Two common rules choose $M$:

- **Elbow.** Keep the components before the scree plot flattens. Here the
PVE falls by a factor of 22 from
component 3 to component 4, the largest ratio between
consecutive components, so
$M = 3$.
- **Cumulative threshold.** Keep the fewest components whose cumulative PVE
reaches a chosen level. At 90% (dotted line), $M = 3$; the first
2 reach 88.1%.

Both are judgments: the elbow is read from a picture, and the threshold is a
choice. Neither looks at the price. When the components are used to predict a
response, the next lecture chooses $M$ by cross-validation instead.

### Unstandardized components

Principal components of the centered but unstandardized explanatory
variables maximize $a^\top\mathbf{S}a$, with $\mathbf{S}$ the sample
covariance matrix, whose diagonal holds the squared standard deviations
above. The figure compares the first loading vector of the standardized
features with that of the unstandardized variables, and with that of the
unstandardized variables after weight is recorded in milligrams
(1 carat = 200 mg) instead of carats.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Code

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# First loading vector of a covariance or correlation matrix, signed so its
# largest loading in absolute value is positive.
signed_pc1 <- function(M) {
  phi <- eigen(M, symmetric = TRUE)$vectors[, 1]
  phi * largest_sign(phi)
}

# Explanatory variables with weight in milligrams instead of carats.
X_mg <- X
X_mg[, "carat"] <- 200 * X_mg[, "carat"]
mg_sd <- sd_n(X_mg[, "carat"])

# Covariance matrices, divisor n, in carats and in milligrams.
S <- cov(X) * (n - 1) / n
S_mg <- cov(X_mg) * (n - 1) / n

# Unstandardized first loading vectors and the PVE of their components.
pc1_raw <- signed_pc1(S)
pc1_mg <- signed_pc1(S_mg)
pve_raw <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE)$values[1] / sum(diag(S))
pve_mg <- eigen(S_mg, symmetric = TRUE)$values[1] / sum(diag(S_mg))

# Standardized first loading vector in milligrams, and its largest
# difference from the one in carats.
pc1_mg_std <- signed_pc1(cor(X_mg))
pc1_mg_gap <- max(abs(pc1_mg_std - Phi[, 1]))

# Facet labels: each version and the PVE of its first component.
pc1_versions <- c("Standardized",
                  "Unstandardized",
                  "Unstandardized, carat in mg")
pc1_pve <- c(pve[1], pve_raw, pve_mg)
version_labels <- paste0(pc1_versions, "\nPVE ", pct(pc1_pve))

# First loading vector of each version, one facet each.
version_rep <- rep(version_labels, each = p)
feature_rep <- rep(features, 3)
feature_levels <- rev(features)
scaling_data <- tibble(version = factor(version_rep, levels = version_labels),
                       feature = factor(feature_rep, levels = feature_levels),
                       loading = c(Phi[, 1], pc1_raw, pc1_mg))
scaling_plot <- ggplot(scaling_data, aes(x = loading, y = feature)) +
  loading_bars +
  facet_wrap(~ version) +
  labs(x = "Loading on the first component",
       y = NULL,
       title = title_all)
```
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](40-principal-components_files/figure-html/scaling-figure-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


Unstandardized, the first component is mostly table, loading
0.92, the variable with the largest variance,
and it no longer measures size. Recording weight in milligrams raises the

Standardized features remove the dependence on units: the correlation matrix
is the same in carats or milligrams, and the standardized first loading

features are therefore standardized before principal component analysis
unless the explanatory variables share a unit in which their variances are
comparable, as the three dimensions in mm would on their own. Like the means
and standard deviations of the ridge and lasso lectures, the loadings are
computed from the data, so when components feed a model that is
cross-validated, the standardization and the loadings are recomputed from the
training folds in each fold.

A loading is the weight a feature receives in the component's score. Each is

- **PC1, size.** Carat, `x`, `y`, and `z` load
0.49 to 0.50, table
0.12, and depth 0.00. Four perfectly

dimensions in PC4, whose carat loading is 0.87. Their
variances are small because the four measurements rarely disagree.

### Sign

$\phi_m$ and $-\phi_m$ have the same length and give scores with the same
variance, $\left(-\phi_m\right)^\top\mathbf{R}\left(-\phi_m\right) = \phi_m^\top\mathbf{R}\phi_m$,
so the sign of a loading vector is arbitrary. Flipping it flips every loading
and every score of that component and changes no interpretation: "high PC2 is
deep and narrow-topped" becomes "low PC2 is deep and narrow-topped." This
chapter flips each vector so that its largest loading in absolute value is
positive; `prcomp()` and other software may return either sign.

### Prediction

Principal component analysis is **unsupervised**: the loadings, the scores,
and the variances are computed from the features alone, and the components
are ordered by the variance of the features, not by any relation to a
response. The component with the largest variance need not be the most
useful for prediction, a component with little variance, such as
PC4 here, can carry information about the response that the
first few do not, and a rule that keeps the first $M$ components by PVE can
discard it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Least squares regression of price on all six scores, and its R^2.
price_fit <- lm(kept$price ~ Z)
r2_scores <- summary(price_fit)$r.squared
```
:::


Because the scores of different components are uncorrelated, the squared
correlations of price with the six scores add: they sum to
0.861, which equals the $R^2$ of the least squares
regression of price on all six scores, 0.861. Of that total,
PC4 accounts for 0.046, and PC2 and
PC3 together for 0.010.

Principal components are also **not variable selection**. Every component is
a combination of all $p$ features. Even the smallest loading in absolute
value, that of `depth` on PC1, is
$4.6 \times 10^{-5}$, not zero, so computing even the first score
of a new diamond requires all six explanatory variables, however few
components a model keeps.

## Conclusion

Principal component analysis replaces $p$ correlated features by new
variables, the components, ordered by how much of the features' variance
each carries. The features are the standardized explanatory variables. The
first component's loading vector $\phi_1$ is the unit vector that maximizes
the sample variance of the scores $z_{i1} = \tilde x_i\phi_1$; a Lagrange
multiplier shows that it is the eigenvector of the sample correlation matrix
with the largest eigenvalue, and the eigenvalue is the variance of the
scores. The same direction minimizes the mean squared distance from the data
to a line, because the variance and that distance sum to $p$.

The later components are the remaining eigenvectors, orthogonal directions of
decreasing variance. Their scores are uncorrelated, and their variances sum
to $p$, so the proportion of variance explained by component $m$ is $v_m/p$.
The number of components $M$ kept is the dimension of the reduced feature
set; a scree plot's elbow or a cumulative PVE threshold chooses it by
judgment. Components depend on the units of the explanatory variables, so
the features are standardized unless the units are comparable. A component is
interpreted from its loadings, whose overall sign is arbitrary.

The components are computed without the response. The component with the
most variance need not be the best predictor, a low-variance component can
matter for prediction, and every component uses every feature.

The next lecture, principal components regression and partial least
squares, regresses the log price of the same diamonds on the first $M$
components, chooses $M$ by cross-validation, and compares the components with
directions that partial least squares chooses using the response.
